_comment: A plain-language line for each requirement listed, shown beside its framework's own words in the report, never in place of them (backlog 0372). Written for ASVS 5.0's level-1 and level-2 requirements, every AISVS 1.0 requirement and its Appendix C's, and every control of the Secure by Design checklist; ASVS's level-3 requirements are still to come (backlog 0372). Read through sv_frameworks::data; held to each requirement's own words by crates/sv-report/tests/plain_requirements.rs.

plain.V1.1.1: Input is decoded into its plain form once, only when encoded data is expected, and before it is validated or cleaned, never after.
plain.V1.1.2: Output encoding and escaping happen as the last step before the data is used by its interpreter, or by the interpreter itself.
plain.V1.2.1: Text the app puts into a page, a header, or an XML document is encoded for the exact place it goes, so it cannot change the page's structure.
plain.V1.2.2: Untrusted data put into a web address is encoded for where it goes in the address, and only safe kinds of address (never javascript: or data:) are allowed.
plain.V1.2.3: Untrusted data put into JavaScript or JSON the app builds is encoded or escaped, so it cannot change the script's or the JSON's structure.
plain.V1.2.4: Database queries keep the data apart from the query itself (parameterized queries, an ORM, or something as safe), so nobody can inject their own query.
plain.V1.2.5: The app never lets input become part of an operating-system command: commands are given their arguments separately, or the input is encoded for the command line.
plain.V1.2.6: The app protects against LDAP injection, so nobody can change a directory query with what they type.
plain.V1.2.7: XPath queries are parameterized or precompiled, so input cannot change what the query asks (XPath injection).
plain.V1.2.8: Any LaTeX processor runs securely, without --shell-escape and with an allowlist of commands, to prevent LaTeX injection.
plain.V1.2.9: Special characters put into a regular expression are escaped, so they are not read as metacharacters.
plain.V1.3.1: HTML that people write in a rich-text editor is cleaned with a well-known, secure HTML sanitizing library or framework feature before it is used.
plain.V1.3.2: The app does not run text as code (eval, SpEL, and the like); where there is truly no alternative, any user input in it is sanitized first.
plain.V1.3.3: Data passed to a potentially dangerous place is sanitized first: only characters safe there are allowed, and input that is too long is trimmed.
plain.V1.3.4: SVG images people upload are validated or sanitized to keep only safe tags and attributes, with no scripts or foreignObject.
plain.V1.3.5: Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or other template text people supply is sanitized, or its scripting is disabled.
plain.V1.3.6: When the app calls another service with untrusted data, the protocol, domain, path, and port are checked against an allowlist, so it cannot be steered elsewhere (server-side request forgery, SSRF).
plain.V1.3.7: Templates are never built from untrusted input; where there is no alternative, the input is sanitized or strictly validated, to stop template injection.
plain.V1.3.8: Untrusted input is sanitized before JNDI queries, and JNDI is configured securely to prevent JNDI injection.
plain.V1.3.9: Content is sanitized before it is sent to memcache, to prevent injection.
plain.V1.3.10: Format strings that could resolve in an unexpected or malicious way are sanitized before they are processed.
plain.V1.3.11: Input is sanitized before it reaches a mail system, to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection.
plain.V1.4.1: The code uses memory-safe strings, safer memory copies, and checked pointer arithmetic, to prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.
plain.V1.4.2: Sign, range, and input checks prevent integer overflows.
plain.V1.4.3: Memory and resources are released when done, and pointers to freed memory are removed or set to null, to prevent use-after-free bugs.
plain.V1.5.1: XML parsers are set up restrictively, with dangerous features such as external entities turned off, so XML cannot be used for an XXE attack.
plain.V1.5.2: Deserialization of untrusted data is safe, for example with an allowlist of object types, and deserialization known to be insecure is never used on it.
plain.V2.1.1: The app's documentation says what valid data looks like for each kind of input: an email address, a phone number, a card number, or the app's own formats.
plain.V2.1.2: The documentation says how to check that related pieces of data make sense together, such as a suburb matching its ZIP code.
plain.V2.1.3: The documentation sets out the business logic limits and validations, per user and across the whole application.
plain.V2.2.1: Input is checked against what the app expects (allowed values, patterns, ranges, or structure); at level 1, at least the input used to make business or security decisions.
plain.V2.2.2: Input is validated on the server, the trusted side; checks in the browser help people but are never relied on for security.
plain.V2.2.3: The app checks that combinations of related data items are reasonable, by the rules set out beforehand.
plain.V2.3.1: A multi-step process, such as a checkout, runs its steps in order for the same user, and no step can be skipped.
plain.V2.3.2: The business logic limits the documentation sets out are enforced in the application, so they cannot be exploited.
plain.V2.3.3: Business operations use transactions: each succeeds as a whole or is rolled back to the previous correct state.
plain.V2.3.4: Limited resources, such as theater seats or delivery slots, are locked while being taken, so they cannot be double-booked.
plain.V2.4.1: Anti-automation controls stop excessive calls to the application's functions, which could leak data, fill it with garbage, use up quotas or costly resources, or deny service.
plain.V3.2.1: The browser cannot be tricked into showing a response in the wrong context, such as an API response or an uploaded file opened directly as a page.
plain.V3.2.2: Content meant to be shown as text is put on the page with safe functions (such as textContent), so it can never run as HTML or JavaScript.
plain.V3.3.1: Cookies have the Secure attribute, so they are only sent over HTTPS, and their names use the __Host- or __Secure- prefix.
plain.V3.3.2: Each cookie's SameSite attribute is set to suit its purpose, to limit cross-site request forgery (CSRF) and clickjacking.
plain.V3.3.3: Cookie names start with __Host- unless the cookie is meant to be shared with other hosts.
plain.V3.3.4: A cookie that scripts in the page have no need to read, such as a session token, has the HttpOnly attribute, and its value is only ever sent in the Set-Cookie header.
plain.V3.4.1: Every response tells browsers to use only HTTPS for this site (the Strict-Transport-Security header), for at least a year.
plain.V3.4.2: Cross-origin access (CORS) is allowed only for a fixed origin or origins on an allowlist; when any origin is allowed, the response holds nothing sensitive.
plain.V3.4.3: Every response has a Content-Security-Policy header that only lets the browser load and run trusted content, at least with object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none', and an allowlist, nonces, or hashes.
plain.V3.4.4: Every response has the header X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so browsers never guess a response's type.
plain.V3.4.5: The app sets a referrer policy, so addresses with sensitive data in them are not leaked to other sites through the Referer header.
plain.V3.4.6: Every response's Content-Security-Policy has a frame-ancestors directive, so other sites cannot embed the app's pages unless that is intended.
plain.V3.5.1: Requests that do something sensitive are checked to come from the app itself (with an anti-forgery token or a special header), to stop cross-site request forgery (CSRF), unless the CORS preflight already does that.
plain.V3.5.2: Where the app relies on the browser's CORS preflight to block other sites, sensitive actions cannot be reached by a request that skips the preflight.
plain.V3.5.3: Sensitive actions use POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, never GET or another method meant to be safe, or the request's Sec-Fetch headers are checked strictly instead.
plain.V3.5.4: Separate applications are hosted on different hostnames, so the browser's same-origin policy keeps them apart.
plain.V3.5.5: Messages received through postMessage are thrown away if they come from an origin that is not trusted, or are not well formed.
plain.V3.7.1: The app uses only client-side technologies that are still supported and secure, never Flash, ActiveX, Silverlight, Java applets, or the like.
plain.V3.7.2: The app redirects people automatically to another site it does not control only when that destination is on an allowlist.
plain.V4.1.1: Every response with a body says what kind of content it is (the Content-Type header) and matches it, including the character set, such as UTF-8.
plain.V4.1.2: Only pages people open in a browser redirect from HTTP to HTTPS; other endpoints do not, so a client sending unencrypted requests is noticed.
plain.V4.1.3: Header fields that a proxy or load balancer sets, such as X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP, cannot be overridden by the end user.
plain.V4.2.1: Every component, from load balancer to application server, decides where each HTTP message ends in the same correct way, to prevent HTTP request smuggling.
plain.V4.3.1: GraphQL queries are limited by an allowlist, depth, amount, or cost, so an expensive nested query cannot deny service.
plain.V4.3.2: GraphQL introspection is disabled in production, unless the API is meant to be used by other parties.
plain.V4.4.1: Every WebSocket connection is encrypted (wss://, WebSocket over TLS).
plain.V4.4.2: When a WebSocket connection opens, its Origin header is checked against a list of allowed origins.
plain.V4.4.3: If the app's normal sessions cannot be used for WebSockets, dedicated tokens are used that meet the same session management requirements.
plain.V4.4.4: Dedicated WebSocket session tokens are first obtained or checked through the HTTPS session the person already signed in with.
plain.V5.1.1: The documentation sets, for each upload feature, the allowed file types and extensions, the largest size (unpacked too), and how files are made safe to download, including what happens to a malicious one.
plain.V5.2.1: The app accepts only files small enough to process without slowing down or being knocked over.
plain.V5.2.2: An uploaded file's extension is one the app expects, and its contents really are that type (checking its first bytes, for example); at level 1, at least files used for business or security decisions.
plain.V5.2.3: Before unpacking a compressed file (zip, gz, docx, odt), the app checks its unpacked size and number of files against set limits.
plain.V5.3.1: Files that people upload into a public folder can never be run as code on the server when someone opens their address.
plain.V5.3.2: File paths are built from names the app makes or trusts, not names people send; if a user's file name must be used, it is strictly checked, so nobody can reach other files or servers.
plain.V5.4.1: File names people submit are validated or ignored, and the app sets the file name itself in the Content-Disposition header of the response.
plain.V5.4.2: File names the app serves, in headers or email attachments, are encoded or sanitized (as RFC 6266 describes), so they cannot inject anything.
plain.V5.4.3: Files from untrusted sources are scanned by an antivirus scanner, so known malicious files are not served.
plain.V6.1.1: The documentation says how the app defends sign-in against password guessing and stolen-password lists (rate limiting and the like), how that is set up, and how it avoids locking real users out.
plain.V6.1.2: A list of words specific to the app, such as the organization's and products' names, is documented, so they can be kept out of passwords.
plain.V6.1.3: If there are several ways to sign in, the documentation lists them all, with the security controls and strength each must enforce consistently.
plain.V6.2.1: Passwords people choose are at least 8 characters long; at least 15 is strongly recommended.
plain.V6.2.3: Changing a password asks for the current password as well as the new one.
plain.V6.2.4: A new or changed password is checked against at least the 3,000 most common passwords that fit the app's rules, and refused if it is one of them.
plain.V6.2.5: Passwords can contain any characters, with no rules demanding upper case, numbers, or symbols.
plain.V6.2.6: Password fields hide what is typed (type=password); the app may let people show it for a moment.
plain.V6.2.7: People can paste passwords and use the browser's or another password manager.
plain.V6.2.8: The password is checked exactly as typed, never cut short or changed to lower or upper case.
plain.V6.2.9: Passwords of at least 64 characters are allowed.
plain.V6.2.10: A password stays valid until it is found to be compromised or the user changes it; people are never made to change passwords on a schedule.
plain.V6.2.11: The documented list of words specific to the app is used to stop easy-to-guess passwords being created.
plain.V6.2.12: Passwords chosen at registration or when changing a password are checked against a set of breached passwords.
plain.V6.3.1: The defenses against password guessing and stolen-password lists are in place, as the app's documentation says they are.
plain.V6.3.2: There are no default accounts such as root, admin, or sa, or they are turned off.
plain.V6.3.3: Signing in to the application takes multi-factor authentication, or a combination of single-factor methods.
plain.V6.3.4: If there are several ways to sign in, none is undocumented, and each enforces the same security controls and strength.
plain.V6.4.1: First passwords and activation codes the system makes are random, follow the password rules, expire soon or after first use, and cannot be kept as the long-term password.
plain.V6.4.2: There are no password hints or secret questions.
plain.V6.4.3: Resetting a forgotten password is secure and never skips multi-factor authentication that is turned on.
plain.V6.4.4: When someone loses a multi-factor authentication factor, their identity is checked again as thoroughly as when they first enrolled.
plain.V6.5.1: Lookup secrets, codes sent out of band, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) work only once.
plain.V6.5.2: Lookup secrets with less than 112 bits of entropy are stored hashed with an approved password hashing algorithm and a 32-bit random salt.
plain.V6.5.3: Lookup secrets, out-of-band codes, and time-based one-time password seeds come from a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG), so they cannot be predicted.
plain.V6.5.4: Lookup secrets and out-of-band authentication codes have at least 20 bits of entropy (6 random digits is usually enough).
plain.V6.5.5: Out-of-band authentication codes expire within 10 minutes, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTP) within 30 seconds.
plain.V6.6.1: One-time passwords by phone or SMS are offered only to a phone number already validated, alongside a stronger method, with their risks explained to users.
plain.V6.6.2: An out-of-band authentication code is bound to the sign-in that asked for it, and cannot be used for a previous or later one.
plain.V6.6.3: Out-of-band authentication codes are protected against brute force guessing by rate limiting.
plain.V6.8.1: With several identity providers (IdPs), a user's identity cannot be spoofed through another provider: users are told apart by the provider's ID and their ID there together.
plain.V6.8.2: The digital signatures on authentication assertions, such as JWTs or SAML assertions, are always validated, and any unsigned or wrongly signed one is rejected.
plain.V6.8.3: Each SAML assertion is processed only once within its validity period, to prevent replay attacks.
plain.V6.8.4: When an outside identity provider (IdP) signs people in and a function needs a certain strength or recentness of authentication, the app checks it in what the IdP returns, or assumes the weakest.
plain.V7.1.1: The documentation sets the session inactivity timeout and the absolute maximum session lifetime, and justifies any difference from NIST SP 800-63B's re-authentication rules.
plain.V7.1.2: The documentation says how many sessions one account may have at once, and what happens when the maximum number is reached.
plain.V7.1.3: Every system that creates or manages sessions in a federated setup, such as single sign-on (SSO), is documented, with how session lifetimes, termination, and re-authentication are coordinated.
plain.V7.2.1: Session tokens are checked on the server, the trusted side, every time.
plain.V7.2.2: Sessions use tokens made fresh for each session, never a fixed API key or secret.
plain.V7.2.3: Session tokens that point to data on the server are unique and made by a secure random generator, with at least 128 bits of randomness.
plain.V7.2.4: Signing in, or signing in again, gives a new session token and ends the old one.
plain.V7.3.1: An inactivity timeout makes people authenticate again, as the risk analysis and documented decisions set.
plain.V7.3.2: An absolute maximum session lifetime makes people authenticate again, as the risk analysis and documented decisions set.
plain.V7.4.1: Once a session ends (signing out, or it expires), it cannot be used again; the server forgets it, or self-contained tokens are refused after that point.
plain.V7.4.2: When an account is disabled or deleted, all of its active sessions end.
plain.V7.4.3: After a password or other authentication factor is changed or removed, the user is offered the choice to end all their other active sessions.
plain.V7.4.4: Every page that requires sign-in has an easy, visible way to log out.
plain.V7.4.5: Administrators can end the active sessions of one user, or of all users.
plain.V7.5.1: Changing anything that affects authentication or account recovery, such as the email address, phone number, or multi-factor settings, requires full re-authentication.
plain.V7.5.2: Users can see their active sessions and, after authenticating again, end any or all of them.
plain.V7.6.1: Sessions between the app and an identity provider (IdP) last and end as documented, requiring re-authentication when needed.
plain.V7.6.2: A new application session is created only with the user's consent or an explicit action, never silently.
plain.V8.1.1: The documentation sets out who may use which functions, and who may see or change which records.
plain.V8.1.2: The authorization documentation sets rules for which fields of a record each user may read and write, by their permissions and the record's attributes.
plain.V8.2.1: Each function can be used only by people who have been given permission for it.
plain.V8.2.2: Each record can be reached only by people who have been given permission for that record, so nobody can open someone else's by changing an id in the address.
plain.V8.2.3: Access to individual fields is restricted to users with explicit permission for those fields (broken object property level authorization, BOPLA).
plain.V8.3.1: Who may do what is enforced on the server, never by things a user could change, such as hidden buttons or JavaScript in the browser.
plain.V8.4.1: In an app shared by several customer organizations (tenants), cross-tenant controls ensure nothing a user does can affect a tenant they have no permission for.
plain.V9.1.1: A self-contained token, such as a JWT, has its signature checked before anything in it is trusted.
plain.V9.1.2: Self-contained tokens can be made and checked only with algorithms on an allowlist, never the 'none' algorithm.
plain.V9.1.3: The keys used to check self-contained tokens come only from trusted sources set up in advance, never from a source named inside the token.
plain.V9.2.1: A token is accepted only within its validity period; for a JWT, its nbf and exp times are checked.
plain.V9.2.2: A service accepts a token only after checking it is the right type for the purpose: access tokens for authorization, ID Tokens to prove who signed in.
plain.V9.2.3: A service accepts only tokens meant for it (the audience); for JWTs, the 'aud' claim is checked against an allowlist.
plain.V9.2.4: If a token issuer signs tokens for several audiences with one key, each token names its intended audience, so it cannot be reused for another.
plain.V10.1.1: Tokens are sent only to the components that strictly need them; in a backend-for-frontend design, access and refresh tokens stay in the backend.
plain.V10.1.2: The OAuth client accepts values from the authorization server only from a flow the same browser session started, bound by secrets like PKCE's code_verifier, state, or nonce that cannot be guessed.
plain.V10.2.1: In the code flow, the OAuth client is protected against cross-site request forgery (CSRF) by PKCE or by checking the state parameter.
plain.V10.2.2: An OAuth client that works with more than one authorization server defends against mix-up attacks, for example by validating the 'iss' parameter in responses.
plain.V10.3.1: The resource server accepts only access tokens meant for it (the audience), from the token's 'aud' claim or the introspection endpoint.
plain.V10.3.2: The resource server makes its authorization decisions from the access token's delegated claims, such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorization_details', when they are present.
plain.V10.3.3: When the resource server must identify one user from an access token, it uses claims that cannot be reassigned to another user, usually 'iss' and 'sub' together.
plain.V10.3.4: If the resource server needs a certain strength, method, or recentness of authentication, it checks the access token meets it, for example with the 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' claims.
plain.V10.4.1: The authorization server accepts only redirect addresses registered in advance for each client, compared exactly.
plain.V10.4.2: An authorization code can be used only once; a second use is refused, and the tokens issued from it are revoked.
plain.V10.4.3: Authorization codes expire quickly: within 10 minutes at levels 1 and 2.
plain.V10.4.4: Each client may use only the grant types it needs, and never the implicit ('token') or the 'password' grant.
plain.V10.4.5: Refresh tokens for public clients cannot be replayed: they are tied to the client, or rotated so a used one is refused and its family revoked.
plain.V10.4.6: With the code grant, the authorization server requires proof key for code exchange (PKCE): a valid code_challenge, never the 'plain' method, and a checked code_verifier.
plain.V10.4.7: If clients may register themselves without authentication, the authorization server validates their metadata, gets the user's consent, and warns before an untrusted client is authorized.
plain.V10.4.8: Refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, even when their expiration slides forward with use.
plain.V10.4.9: An authorized user can revoke refresh tokens and reference access tokens in the authorization server's interface, against malicious clients or stolen tokens.
plain.V10.4.10: A confidential client is authenticated for its back-channel requests to the authorization server, such as token, pushed authorization (PAR), and revocation requests.
plain.V10.4.11: The authorization server assigns each OAuth client only the scopes it requires.
plain.V10.5.1: The client prevents ID Token replay, for example by checking the token's 'nonce' claim matches the nonce it sent in the authentication request.
plain.V10.5.2: The client identifies the user from ID Token claims that cannot be reassigned to another user, usually 'sub'.
plain.V10.5.3: The client rejects authorization server metadata whose issuer URL does not exactly match the one it expects, so a malicious server cannot impersonate another.
plain.V10.5.4: The client checks an ID Token is meant for it: the token's 'aud' claim must equal the client's own client_id.
plain.V10.5.5: With OIDC back-channel logout, the client checks a logout token is typed 'logout+jwt', has the right 'event' claim, and has no 'nonce', so forced logout and token confusion are prevented.
plain.V10.6.1: The OpenID Provider allows only 'code', 'ciba', 'id_token', or 'id_token code' as the response mode, and never 'token' (the implicit flow).
plain.V10.6.2: The OpenID Provider prevents forced logout by getting the user's explicit confirmation, or by validating the logout request's parameters such as 'id_token_hint'.
plain.V10.7.1: The authorization server makes sure the user consents to each authorization request, always asking explicitly when the client's identity cannot be assured.
plain.V10.7.2: When the authorization server asks for consent, it says clearly what is being consented to: what is authorized, to which application, and for how long.
plain.V10.7.3: Users can review, change, and revoke the consents they gave through the authorization server.
plain.V11.1.1: A documented policy manages cryptographic keys through their whole lifecycle, following a standard such as NIST SP 800-57, and keys are not shared more widely than needed.
plain.V11.1.2: An up-to-date cryptographic inventory lists every key, algorithm, and certificate the application uses, where each may be used, and what data each may protect.
plain.V11.2.1: Cryptographic operations use industry-validated implementations, such as well-known libraries or hardware, never home-made ones.
plain.V11.2.2: The application is built so its cryptographic algorithms, key lengths, and modes can be swapped or upgraded at any time, and keys and passwords replaced and data re-encrypted (crypto agility).
plain.V11.2.3: Every cryptographic primitive gives at least 128 bits of security, for example a 256-bit ECC key or a 3072-bit RSA key.
plain.V11.3.1: Insecure encryption modes such as ECB, and weak padding such as PKCS#1 v1.5, are not used.
plain.V11.3.2: Only approved ciphers and modes, such as AES with GCM, are used.
plain.V11.3.3: Encrypted data is protected against unauthorized changes, preferably with approved authenticated encryption, or with encryption plus an approved MAC.
plain.V11.4.1: Only approved hash functions are used for cryptography; MD5 and the like are never used for any cryptographic purpose.
plain.V11.4.2: Passwords are stored with an approved, deliberately slow key derivation function (a password hashing function), with settings that follow current guidance to make brute-force attacks hard.
plain.V11.4.3: Hash functions used for digital signatures and data integrity are collision resistant, with outputs of at least 256 bits where collision resistance is needed.
plain.V11.4.4: Keys derived from passwords use an approved key derivation function with key stretching, set strongly enough that brute force cannot recover the key.
plain.V11.5.1: Every random number or string meant to be unguessable comes from a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG) and has at least 128 bits of entropy; a UUID does not count.
plain.V11.6.1: Only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes are used to generate keys and to make and check digital signatures, and no generated key is weak to known attacks.
plain.V12.1.1: Only the latest recommended TLS versions, such as 1.2 and 1.3, are turned on, with the newest preferred.
plain.V12.1.2: Only recommended TLS cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest preferred.
plain.V12.1.3: Before an mTLS client certificate's identity is used to authenticate or authorize, the application checks the certificate is trusted.
plain.V12.2.1: All connections from clients to the app's public web services use TLS, and never fall back to unencrypted connections.
plain.V12.2.2: The app's public services use TLS certificates that browsers trust.
plain.V12.3.1: Every connection to and from the application, including to databases, monitoring, administration, partner systems, and outside APIs, uses an encrypted protocol such as TLS, never falling back to an unencrypted one.
plain.V12.3.2: When the application connects to a TLS server, it validates the server's certificate first.
plain.V12.3.3: Connections between the application's own HTTP-based services use TLS or similar transport encryption, never falling back to unencrypted communication.
plain.V12.3.4: TLS between internal services uses trusted certificates; where internal or self-signed certificates are used, each service trusts only those specific ones.
plain.V13.1.1: Every communication need of the application is documented, including the external services it relies on and any place a user could point it to connect to.
plain.V13.2.1: The application's backend components (APIs, middleware, data layers) authenticate to each other with individual service accounts, short-lived tokens, or certificates, never fixed passwords or shared API keys.
plain.V13.2.2: Backend components, operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers talk to each other with accounts that have the least privileges they need.
plain.V13.2.3: When a credential is used for one service to authenticate to another, it is never a default credential such as admin/admin.
plain.V13.2.4: An allowlist sets which outside resources and systems the application may communicate with, for requests, data loads, and file access.
plain.V13.2.5: The web or application server is configured with an allowlist of the resources and systems it may send requests to or load data and files from.
plain.V13.3.1: Backend secrets, such as passwords, keys, and API keys, are created, stored, accessed, and destroyed through a secrets management solution such as a key vault, never in the source code or build artifacts.
plain.V13.3.2: Access to secrets follows the principle of least privilege.
plain.V13.4.1: The app is deployed without its source control folders (.git, .svn), or they cannot be reached, from outside or by the app itself.
plain.V13.4.2: Debug modes are disabled for every component in production, so debugging features and information do not leak.
plain.V13.4.3: Web servers do not show directory listings unless that is explicitly intended.
plain.V13.4.4: The HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production, so it cannot leak information.
plain.V13.4.5: Documentation, such as for internal APIs, and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless that is explicitly intended.
plain.V14.1.1: All sensitive data the application creates or handles is identified and classified into protection levels, including data only encoded (such as Base64 or a JWT's payload), with the regulations it must follow in mind.
plain.V14.1.2: Each protection level for sensitive data has documented requirements: encryption, integrity, retention, logging, access to logs, database encryption, privacy, and other confidentiality needs.
plain.V14.2.1: Sensitive data, such as an API key or a session token, is sent only in the body or the headers of a request, never in the web address.
plain.V14.2.2: Sensitive data is not cached in server components such as load balancers and application caches, or it is securely purged after use.
plain.V14.2.3: Sensitive data is never sent to untrusted parties, such as user trackers, where it would be collected outside the application's control.
plain.V14.2.4: The controls for sensitive data (encryption, integrity, retention, logging, privacy) are implemented as the documentation sets them for that data's protection level.
plain.V14.3.1: Signed-in data is cleared from the browser when the session ends, even when the server cannot be reached.
plain.V14.3.2: Responses carrying sensitive data set anti-caching headers (Cache-Control: no-store), so browsers do not cache it.
plain.V14.3.3: Browser storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies) holds no sensitive data, apart from session tokens.
plain.V15.1.1: The documentation sets deadlines for fixing third-party components with known weaknesses, and for keeping libraries up to date, by how risky they are.
plain.V15.1.2: An inventory, such as a software bill of materials (SBOM), lists every third-party library in use, and checks each comes from a trusted, maintained repository.
plain.V15.1.3: The documentation names the functions that are slow or use many resources, and how to keep them from making the app unavailable or taking longer than the consumer's timeout.
plain.V15.2.1: Every component the app ships is within the update and fix deadlines its documentation sets.
plain.V15.2.2: The application defends against slow or resource-heavy functions making it unavailable, as the documented decisions set out.
plain.V15.2.3: The production environment holds only the functionality the application needs, with no test code, sample snippets, or development features exposed.
plain.V15.3.1: The app returns only the fields of a record that are needed, never the whole record with fields some users must not see.
plain.V15.3.2: When the backend calls outside addresses, it does not follow redirects unless that is intended.
plain.V15.3.3: The application protects against mass assignment by limiting which fields each action may set, so a field not meant to be changed by an action cannot be.
plain.V15.3.4: Proxies and middleware pass on the user's original IP address in trusted fields the user cannot manipulate, and the app uses that value for logging and rate limiting.
plain.V15.3.5: The code checks variables are of the correct type and uses strict equality and comparisons, so type juggling or type confusion cannot be exploited.
plain.V15.3.6: JavaScript code is written to prevent prototype pollution, for example by using Map() or Set() instead of plain object literals.
plain.V15.3.7: The application defends against HTTP parameter pollution, especially where its framework does not tell apart parameters from the query string, body, cookies, and header fields.
plain.V16.1.1: An inventory documents the logging at each layer: what events are logged, the formats, where logs are stored, how they are used, who can access them, and how long they are kept.
plain.V16.2.1: Each log entry has the metadata needed to investigate an event's timeline: when, where, who, and what.
plain.V16.2.2: All logging components use synchronized time sources, and security event timestamps are in UTC or carry an explicit time zone offset.
plain.V16.2.3: Logs are stored or sent only to the files and services the log inventory documents.
plain.V16.2.4: Logs can be read and correlated by the log processor in use, preferably by using a common logging format.
plain.V16.2.5: Sensitive data is logged only as its protection level allows: some, such as credentials or payment details, never; others, such as session tokens, only hashed or masked.
plain.V16.3.1: Every authentication operation is logged, successful and unsuccessful, preferably with the type of authentication or factors used.
plain.V16.3.3: The security events the documentation defines are logged, as are attempts to bypass security controls such as input validation, business logic, and anti-automation.
plain.V16.3.4: Unexpected errors and security control failures, such as a backend TLS failure, are logged.
plain.V16.4.1: Every logging component encodes data appropriately to prevent log injection.
plain.V16.4.2: Logs are protected from unauthorized access and cannot be modified.
plain.V16.4.3: Logs are sent securely to a logically separate system for analysis and alerting, so a breach of the application does not compromise them.
plain.V16.5.1: When an unexpected or security-sensitive error occurs, the app returns a generic message, never internal details such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, or tokens.
plain.V16.5.2: The application keeps operating securely when an outside resource fails, for example with circuit breakers or graceful degradation.
plain.V16.5.3: The application fails gracefully and securely, including on an exception, so it never fails open, such as completing a transaction despite a validation error.
plain.V17.1.1: The TURN relay service allows access only to IP addresses that are not reserved for special purposes, such as internal networks, broadcast, or loopback, in IPv4 and IPv6.
plain.V17.2.1: The key for the DTLS certificate is managed and protected as the documented policy for cryptographic keys sets.
plain.V17.2.2: The media server uses approved Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) cipher suites and a secure DTLS-SRTP protection profile.
plain.V17.2.3: The media server checks SRTP authentication, so injected RTP packets cannot deny service or insert audio or video into a stream.
plain.V17.2.4: The media server keeps processing incoming media traffic when it receives malformed Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets.
plain.V17.3.1: The signaling server keeps processing legitimate signaling messages during a flood, through rate limiting at the signaling level.
plain.V17.3.2: The signaling server keeps processing legitimate signaling messages when a malformed one arrives, through input validation and robust error handling.
plain.C1.1.1: Training data includes only the features, attributes, and fields the model needs for its stated purpose.
plain.C1.1.2: An up-to-date inventory lists every training-data source with its origin, responsible party, license, collection method, intended use constraints, and processing history.
plain.C1.1.3: The integrity of training data (that it has not been changed) is protected while it is stored and while it is transferred.
plain.C1.1.4: Training data is monitored for integrity, to guard against unauthorized modifications or corruption.
plain.C1.1.5: Datasets are watermarked (marked in a hidden, traceable way) so their use can be attributed and any unauthorized use detected.
plain.C1.2.1: Labeling platforms (where people tag training data) enforce access controls on who can create, modify, or approve annotations.
plain.C1.2.2: Labeling artifacts (the files of labels and annotations) carry cryptographic integrity protection, so any change to them can be detected.
plain.C1.2.3: Sensitive information in labels is redacted, anonymized, or encrypted before it is used in any labeling artifact.
plain.C1.3.1: Training and fine-tuning pipelines use poisoning detection to find data poisoning (deliberately planted bad data) or unintentional corruption in training data.
plain.C1.3.2: Automatically generated labels pass confidence thresholds and consistency checks, to detect misleading or low-confidence labels.
plain.C1.3.3: Models used in security-relevant decisions are evaluated for bias patterns.
plain.C1.3.4: Disallowed content is detected and removed from the data before training.
plain.C1.3.5: Defenses are in place against clean-label poisoning attacks (bad training examples that look correctly labeled but teach the model a hidden behavior).
plain.C2.1.1: Input is normalized (put into one standard form) before tokenization or embedding, the steps that turn text into what the model reads.
plain.C2.1.2: Encoding and representation smuggling in inputs (hiding instructions in unusual encodings or characters) is detected and mitigated by canonicalization, strict schema validation, policy-based rejection, or explicit marking.
plain.C2.1.3: All inputs that could steer model behavior are treated as untrusted and screened by a prompt injection (text written to make the AI ignore its instructions) ruleset or classifier, and flagged inputs are blocked.
plain.C2.1.4: Input length controls keep content from exceeding the model's context window (how much text it can read at once), and inputs over the token limits are rejected, not truncated.
plain.C2.1.5: The system restricts the character set of all inputs with an allow-list that permits only the characters that are explicitly required.
plain.C2.1.6: The system enforces an instruction hierarchy: system and developer messages override user instructions and other untrusted inputs, even after user instructions have been processed.
plain.C2.1.7: Reserved special tokens (control markers the model treats specially) are encoded as literal characters, so they cannot be injected into the model context.
plain.C2.1.8: The system can detect many-shot jailbreaking patterns (long runs of example dialogue meant to wear down the AI's rules).
plain.C2.2.1: Every prompt is scored by a content classifier for violence, self-harm, hate, and sexual content against configurable thresholds, and prompts over a threshold are rejected or sanitized before reaching the model context.
plain.C2.2.2: Prompt content classification is evaluated for how it handles unsupported languages.
plain.C2.2.3: Non-text inputs (image, video, and audio) are checked for adversarial perturbations, steganographic payloads (hidden messages), hidden or embedded content, or known attack patterns.
plain.C2.2.4: Coordinated attacks spanning multiple input types, such as a hidden payload in an image combined with prompt injection in text, are detected and blocked.
plain.C3.1.1: A model registry keeps an inventory of all deployed model artifacts and their origin.
plain.C3.1.2: All model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, base models, fine-tunes, adapters, and safety or policy models) are cryptographically signed by authorized entities.
plain.C3.1.3: Model cryptographic signatures are verified when a model is admitted for deployment and again when it is loaded.
plain.C3.2.1: Before deployment, models undergo automated input validation testing, safety evaluation testing, and output sanitization testing.
plain.C3.2.2: A model shrunk by post-training quantization is re-evaluated on the compressed artifact, against the same safety and alignment test suite, before deployment.
plain.C3.2.3: A change to the provider's model, version, or routing triggers a security re-evaluation before the model's continued use.
plain.C3.3.1: Production deployments use rollout mechanisms with automated rollback triggers, which return to the previous version when something goes wrong.
plain.C3.3.2: Rollback capabilities restore the complete model state.
plain.C3.3.3: Model versions running in parallel use isolated runtime state, so AI-specific shared resources are not shared across deployments.
plain.C3.4.1: AI-specific runtime components are not shared across environment boundaries, such as development, staging, and production.
plain.C3.4.2: Model training and fine-tuning environments are isolated from production environments.
plain.C3.5.1: Models used in RLHF fine-tuning (training from human feedback) are versioned and integrity-verified before use in a training run.
plain.C3.5.2: RLHF training stages include automated detection of reward hacking or reward model over-optimization, where the model games its scoring instead of improving.
plain.C3.5.3: In multi-stage fine-tuning pipelines, each stage's output is integrity-verified before the next stage consumes it.
plain.C3.5.4: Fine-tuning checkpoints (saved snapshots of a model during training) are registered as distinct artifacts.
plain.C4.1.1: AI models execute in isolated sandboxes.
plain.C4.1.2: Model artifact loading accepts only an explicit allow-list of serialization (file storage) formats that cannot run arbitrary code during deserialization (loading).
plain.C4.1.3: Workload attestation is performed before model loading, to prove the execution environment has not been tampered with.
plain.C4.1.4: Confidential inference services protect model weights while running, through isolated execution environments.
plain.C4.2.1: AI accelerator (GPU) firmware is version-pinned, signed, and attested (proven genuine) at boot.
plain.C4.2.2: Execution within a trusted execution environment (TEE, a sealed-off area of the processor) provides hardware-enforced isolation, memory encryption, and integrity protection.
plain.C4.2.3: AI accelerator (GPU) integrity is validated using hardware-based attestation mechanisms before each workload executes.
plain.C4.2.4: Accelerator (GPU) memory is isolated between workloads through partitioning, and memory is sanitized (wiped) between jobs.
plain.C4.2.5: Accelerator interconnects (the links between GPUs) are restricted to approved topologies and authenticated endpoints.
plain.C4.3.1: Edge AI devices authenticate to central infrastructure using strong authentication mechanisms.
plain.C4.3.2: Models deployed to edge or mobile devices are cryptographically signed during packaging, and the on-device runtime validates these signatures or checksums before loading or inference.
plain.C4.3.3: Inference runtimes (the software that runs the model) enforce process, memory, and file access isolation.
plain.C4.3.4: Model weights and sensitive parameters stored locally are encrypted using hardware-backed key stores or secure enclaves.
plain.C4.3.5: Models packaged within mobile, IoT, or embedded applications are encrypted at rest and decrypted only inside a trusted runtime or secure enclave, preventing direct extraction from the app package or filesystem.
plain.C5.1.1: High-risk AI operations (model deployment, weight export, training data access, and production configuration changes) require step-up authentication, an extra proof of identity at that moment.
plain.C5.1.2: AI agents in federated or multi-system deployments authenticate using short-lived, minimal-scoped, cryptographically signed tokens.
plain.C5.2.1: Every AI resource (datasets, endpoints, vector collections, embedding indices, and compute instances) enforces access controls with explicit allow-lists and default-deny policies.
plain.C5.2.2: Retrieval pipelines (such as RAG queries and embedding lookups) enforce the end-user's own authorization at each retrieval and assembly stage, rather than relying solely on the service account's permissions.
plain.C5.2.3: Sensitive data is retrieved through retrieval pipelines (such as RAG queries and embedding lookups), so it is not permanently stored in models.
plain.C5.2.4: Post-inference filtering keeps responses from including data that the requester is not authorized to receive.
plain.C5.2.5: The policy decision point that decides what an agent is authorized to do is isolated from the agent's execution environment.
plain.C5.2.6: Privileged access to model weights, training pipelines, and production AI configuration is granted just in time, with a defined maximum session duration and automatic expiry; Zero Standing Privilege (no permanent access) is encouraged.
plain.C5.2.7: Data classification labels propagate to downstream resources, such as embeddings, prompt caches, and model outputs.
plain.C5.3.1: Shared model serving infrastructure prevents one tenant's fine-tuning, inference, or embedding operations from influencing or observing another tenant's operations.
plain.C5.3.2: One tenant (a separate customer sharing the same system) cannot influence or observe another tenant's operations through shared compute resources; this typically needs hardware partitioning, confidential computing, or dedicated compute per tenant.
plain.C6.1.1: Models are scanned for malicious code before they are imported.
plain.C6.1.2: Model weights (the trained numbers that make up a model), datasets, and fine-tuning adapters are downloaded only from approved sources.
plain.C6.1.3: Every model artifact (model file) that comes from a third party can be checked for integrity, so any tampering would be noticed.
plain.C6.1.4: Models pass a suite of behavioral acceptance tests before they are promoted to any environment other than development.
plain.C6.2.1: Every model artifact publishes an AI BOM (a parts list for the model) that is version-controlled and machine-readable and lists its datasets, weights, licenses, and statements of where the data came from.
plain.C6.2.2: AI BOMs (parts lists for AI models) are cryptographically signed before deployment, so a change to them can be detected.
plain.C6.2.3: A completeness check on the AI BOM (the model's parts list) fails the build if metadata for any component is missing.
plain.C7.1.1: The application checks all model outputs against a defined schema (a description of the expected format) and rejects any output that does not match.
plain.C7.1.2: Output generated by the model is bounded by length limits and controls that make it stop.
plain.C7.2.1: The system assesses how reliable generated answers are using a confidence estimation method.
plain.C7.2.2: The application automatically blocks an answer, or switches to a fallback message, when its confidence score drops below a defined threshold.
plain.C7.2.3: For responses that the policy classifies as high-risk, the system performs an additional verification step.
plain.C7.3.1: Automated classifiers scan every response and block content that matches the defined categories of harmful content.
plain.C7.3.2: Output filters detect and block responses that disclose the content of the system prompt (the AI's hidden instructions) or backend data.
plain.C7.3.3: Output generated by the model is prevented from triggering outbound requests to other systems.
plain.C7.3.4: Model outputs are checked for hidden, encoded, or misleading content created through homoglyphs (look-alike characters), formatting, metadata, or structured fields.
plain.C7.4.1: Responses generated using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, where the AI answers from documents it looks up) include attribution to the source documents.
plain.C7.4.2: In RAG answers, the source attributions come from the retrieval records and are not generated by the model, so the AI cannot make up where information came from.
plain.C7.4.3: Each claim in a RAG response (an answer built from looked-up documents) can be traced back to the retrieved chunk of text it came from.
plain.C7.4.4: Generated media is watermarked to prove it was AI-generated.
plain.C8.1.1: Vector identifiers and namespaces (the labels for stored AI memory entries) are unique per tenant, so one customer's entries cannot collide with another's.
plain.C8.1.2: Document metadata tags cannot be changed after they are first written.
plain.C8.1.3: Retrieval operations (looking up stored documents for the AI) enforce scope constraints, returning only what is within the allowed scope.
plain.C8.2.1: Sensitive fields are detected before data is embedded (turned into vectors for AI search) and are masked, tokenized, or dropped.
plain.C8.2.2: Vectors that fall outside normal clustering patterns (stored entries that look unusual) are flagged and quarantined before they enter production indices.
plain.C8.2.3: Outputs from agents and tools are not automatically written to trusted agent memory without explicit validation of their source.
plain.C8.2.4: Content crafted to manipulate retrieval results is detected and rejected or quarantined before vectorization (before it is stored for AI search).
plain.C8.2.5: New content written to memory is checked for contradictions with what is already stored, and conflicts trigger alerts.
plain.C8.3.1: Expired vectors (stored AI memory entries past their expiry) are excluded from retrieval results.
plain.C8.3.2: The AI's memory can be reset.
plain.C8.3.3: Quarantined content is retained but excluded from all retrieval results.
plain.C9.1.1: Quotas and timeouts are enforced for each tool, covering things such as CPU, memory, disk, outgoing network traffic, and execution time.
plain.C9.1.2: Budgets for each execution, such as maximum recursion depth, token use, and money spent, are configured and enforced by the runtime.
plain.C9.1.3: A swarm-level kill-switch exists that can halt all active agent instances (running AI agents) at once.
plain.C9.2.1: The agent runtime blocks privileged, high-impact, or irreversible actions until explicit human approval is received and verified.
plain.C9.2.2: Approval requests show the action's full parameters in a standard form, such as diffs, commands, recipients, amounts, resources, and scopes, without cutting them short or changing them unsafely.
plain.C9.2.3: Each high-impact action has a trusted reversibility classification, such as read-only, reversible, externally reversible, or irreversible.
plain.C9.2.4: The agent runtime enforces reversibility classifications by blocking actions, requiring approval, or restricting them, based on their impact and whether they can be reversed.
plain.C9.2.5: Any ability of the AI to modify itself, such as rewriting its prompt, changing its tool list, or updating parameters, is restricted by enforceable boundaries.
plain.C9.2.6: Agentic systems include an AI-augmented review of planned high-risk actions before execution, which adds to, and does not replace, the fixed rule-based policy gate.
plain.C9.2.7: The AI-augmented review is protected against manipulation by hostile inputs and cannot be overridden or bypassed through prompt injection (text written to make the AI ignore its instructions).
plain.C9.2.8: Approvals are cryptographically bound to the action parameters, the requester's identity, the execution context, and a unique single-use nonce (a one-time code).
plain.C9.2.9: Cryptographic keys or credentials used to issue approvals are kept isolated from the agent runtime.
plain.C9.2.10: For chains of actions with several steps or several agents, approval gates enforce the highest-impact reversibility classification found anywhere in the chain.
plain.C9.3.1: Each tool or plugin executes in a least-privilege sandbox (an enclosed space with only the access it needs) or is otherwise isolated from model operations.
plain.C9.3.2: Tool outputs are validated against schemas (descriptions of the expected format).
plain.C9.3.3: Tool manifests (each tool's description file) declare the privileges it requires, its resource limits, and its output validation requirements.
plain.C9.3.4: The runtime enforces the privileges, resource limits, and output validation requirements declared in tool manifests.
plain.C9.3.5: Components that process untrusted data are isolated from tool-calling capabilities, so compromised data processing cannot trigger unauthorized tool calls.
plain.C9.3.6: There is architectural separation between processing untrusted tool outputs and the agent's operations.
plain.C9.3.7: External resources named in model output are checked against an approved allow-list or registry before the agent installs or invokes them.
plain.C9.3.8: Policy violations trigger automated containment of the tool involved.
plain.C9.4.1: Each agent instance has a unique cryptographic identity and authenticates as a principal in its own right (an identity of its own) to downstream systems.
plain.C9.4.2: Actions started by an agent are cryptographically bound to each step of the execution chain, so it cannot later be denied who did what (non-repudiation).
plain.C9.4.3: Agent identity credentials are rotated (replaced with new ones) on a defined schedule.
plain.C9.4.4: Agent state saved between invocations is integrity-protected, so tampering with it would be detected.
plain.C9.5.1: Agent actions are authorized against fine-grained policies, enforced by the runtime, that restrict which tools an agent may invoke and which parameter values it may supply.
plain.C9.5.2: When an agent acts on a user's behalf, the runtime passes along a tamper-protected, scope-limited token that carries the user's authorization and is enforced at every downstream call.
plain.C9.5.3: All access control decisions are enforced by application logic or a policy engine, never by the AI model itself.
plain.C9.5.4: Secrets and credentials an agent needs at runtime are not exposed in anything the model can see, including the context window, system prompts, or tool call parameters.
plain.C9.5.5: Delegation of tasks from one agent to another is restricted by an explicit authorization policy.
plain.C9.5.6: Long-running agent sessions re-check the current backend authorization policy on every privileged action.
plain.C9.6.1: A manual kill-switch mechanism exists to immediately halt AI model inference (the model producing answers) and its outputs.
plain.C9.6.2: When a step that needs a human's approval is not approved within the set approval time, the system blocks the pending action.
plain.C9.6.3: Kill-switch commands (the emergency stop for an AI agent) go through a separate, out-of-band channel that is isolated from where the agent runs.
plain.C10.1.1: MCP components (the add-ons that give an AI tools and data) come only from trusted sources and are checked with cryptography to prove they are genuine.
plain.C10.1.2: Only MCP servers on an approved list (an allow-list) are permitted.
plain.C10.1.3: MCP servers launched locally run in a sandbox with the least privilege needed, with restricted access to the file system, the network, and the system.
plain.C10.2.1: MCP servers check the access token on each request, and do not rely on transport security (such as HTTPS) alone.
plain.C10.2.2: MCP servers check each presented access token's issuer, audience, expiration, and scope claims, following OAuth 2.1.
plain.C10.2.3: MCP servers acting as OAuth 2.1 resource servers do not store or keep access tokens or user credentials.
plain.C10.2.4: The MCP tools/list reply returns only the tools that the resource owners' authorized scopes permit.
plain.C10.2.5: MCP servers enforce access control on every tool call, checking that the user's access token authorizes both the requested tool and the specific argument values supplied.
plain.C10.2.6: MCP servers remove all session artifacts (anything left over from a session) when the session ends.
plain.C10.2.7: MCP servers do not pass the access tokens they receive from clients on to downstream APIs (other services they call).
plain.C10.3.1: MCP traffic to remote services uses authenticated, encrypted streamable HTTP.
plain.C10.3.2: The stdio transport (an MCP connection through a program's standard input and output) is permitted only in controlled local environments.
plain.C10.3.3: On all HTTP-based transports, MCP servers check the Origin header and the Host header separately, to prevent DNS rebinding attacks (tricking a browser into reaching a local server).
plain.C10.3.4: MCP clients enforce a minimum acceptable protocol version and reject initialize responses that propose a version below that minimum.
plain.C10.3.5: Access tokens between the MCP client and server are sender-constrained with mTLS or DPoP, so a stolen token cannot be used by anyone else.
plain.C10.4.1: MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are checked against their declared schemas (their expected format) before being put into the model's context.
plain.C10.4.2: MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are screened for indirect prompt injection (hidden text meant to make the AI ignore its instructions) before being put into the model's context.
plain.C10.4.3: MCP servers reject unrecognized or oversized parameters in function calls.
plain.C10.4.4: All MCP servers enforce strict schema validation (checking that every message matches its expected format exactly).
plain.C10.4.5: All MCP transports enforce a maximum payload size limit on the data they carry.
plain.C10.4.6: MCP servers sign tool responses with a unique nonce (a one-time number) and a timestamp, so MCP clients can detect replay attempts (an old response sent again).
plain.C10.4.7: When a local MCP server is installed, MCP clients show users an explicit consent dialogue with options to cancel.
plain.C10.4.8: MCP clients keep a snapshot of tool definitions, and any change to a tool definition requires re-approval before the modified tool can be used.
plain.C11.1.1: The model has had alignment and safety training or fine-tuning to prevent it from generating disallowed categories of content.
plain.C11.1.2: A version-controlled alignment test suite (tests that the model behaves as intended) is run on every model update or release.
plain.C11.1.3: Models are evaluated against known adversarial attack techniques (deliberate tricks to fool them) relevant to their modality (the kind of input they take, such as text or images).
plain.C11.1.4: Models are hardened against adversarial inputs (input crafted to trick them).
plain.C11.1.5: An automated evaluator measures the rate of harmful content and flags regressions beyond a defined threshold.
plain.C11.2.1: Sensitive attributes that the model infers about people are not directly returned in its outputs.
plain.C11.2.2: Inference endpoints (where the model is queried) enforce rate limits per user or caller and overall, sized against the threat of someone extracting the model, not only as a generic API throttle.
plain.C11.2.3: Model outputs are calibrated to reduce overconfident predictions.
plain.C11.2.4: Training on sensitive datasets uses differentially-private optimization (a method that limits what the model can reveal about any one person in the data).
plain.C11.2.5: Simulated membership-inference attacks (guessing whether a record was in the training data) show that attack accuracy is no better than random guessing on the evaluated data.
plain.C11.3.1: Analysis of query patterns feeds a detector for attempts to extract (copy) the model.
plain.C11.3.2: Raw model outputs are not directly exposed beyond the application backend, and responses visible outside are calibrated to the risk of model extraction (copying).
plain.C11.3.3: Model watermarking or fingerprinting techniques are applied so that unauthorized copies of the model can be identified.
plain.C11.3.4: Detection of a suspected model extraction (copying) attempt triggers response measures.
plain.C11.4.1: Inputs from external or untrusted sources pass through anomaly detection (spotting unusual input) before the model processes them.
plain.C11.4.2: Inputs flagged as anomalous trigger gating actions (steps that hold back or stop the input).
plain.C11.4.3: The pipeline that feeds safety violation reports back into the system includes poisoning detection and human review gates, so attackers cannot manipulate how the system improves.
plain.C12.1.1: AI interactions are logged with session context and AI-specific telemetry (measurements about how the AI was used).
plain.C12.1.2: Safety filtering and policy decisions are logged in enough detail to support audit, debugging, and forensic analysis of content moderation systems.
plain.C12.1.3: Log entries for AI inference events follow a structured, interoperable schema that includes at least the model identifier, token usage (input and output), provider name, and operation type.
plain.C12.1.4: RAG pipeline retrieval events (where the AI looks up documents to answer) are logged, including the query, the documents retrieved, and the knowledge source.
plain.C12.2.1: The system detects and alerts on known jailbreak patterns, prompt injection attempts (text meant to make the AI ignore its instructions), and adversarial inputs.
plain.C12.2.2: Behavioral anomaly detection identifies unusual conversation patterns, excessive retry attempts, or probing behaviors.
plain.C12.2.3: Custom rules detect AI-specific threat patterns for coordinated jailbreak attempts, prompt injection, and attempts to extract the system prompt (the AI's hidden instructions).
plain.C12.2.4: Extraction-alert events include metadata about the offending queries to support investigation.
plain.C12.2.5: Token usage is tracked at detailed levels, including per user, per session, per feature endpoint, and per team or workspace.
plain.C12.2.6: LLM API traffic is monitored for signs of covert channels and known communication signatures, to identify malware and command-and-control (C2) activity.
plain.C12.3.1: Data drift detection monitors changes in input data that may affect model performance, using statistically validated methods matched to the type of data, such as the KS test or PSI for numbers and embedding distance for text or images.
plain.C12.3.2: Hallucination detection monitors identify and flag model outputs that contain factually incorrect, inconsistent, or made-up information.
plain.C12.3.3: Hallucination rates are tracked continuously over time, so trends and sustained model degradation can be detected.
plain.C12.3.4: Unexplained shifts in behavior are told apart from gradual, expected operational drift.
plain.C12.4.1: Triggers for autonomous actions include proactive analysis of behavior patterns, a security evaluation, and an assessment of the threat landscape.
plain.C12.4.2: Audit logs capture security-critical proactive actions, including the approver's identity, the timestamp, the action parameters, and the decision outcomes.
plain.C12.4.3: Kill-switch activations (emergency stops) and override commands are logged.
plain.C12.5.1: Dataset lineage records each dataset and its components, including all transformations, augmentations, and merges.
plain.C12.5.2: All labeling activities on data are recorded in logs.
plain.C12.5.3: All model changes produce immutable audit records (records that cannot be altered).
plain.C12.5.4: Every ingested document is tagged when it is written with its source, the writer's identity, and a timestamp.
plain.AC.1.1: A written workflow says when AI tools may generate, refactor, or review code, and names the approved tools, the prohibited use cases, and the data classifications allowed as input.
plain.AC.1.2: The workflow covers every phase of secure software development (SSDLC), from design and implementation through code review, testing, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring, and names the security gates that stay mandatory with or without AI.
plain.AC.1.3: The workflow names the AI attack scenarios it is built to mitigate: prompt injection through PR content, AI-generated supply-chain payloads, agents approving their own work, secret theft through fork PRs, and a compromised model supply chain.
plain.AC.1.4: Metrics are collected on code that AI produced or handled and compared against a human-only baseline; useful ones include vulnerability density, time to detect, AI-attributable defect rate, prompt-injection detection rate, and fork-PR rejection rate.
plain.AC.2.1: Every AI tool (assistant, reviewer, agent, or MCP server) has a threat model covering misuse, model inversion, training-data leakage, prompt injection, insecure output handling, excessive agency, and risk inherited from its dependencies.
plain.AC.2.2: Each tool's evaluation reviews, in writing, its local components (static and dynamic analysis), its online service endpoints (TLS, sign-in, permissions, logging, and data residency), and the vendor's model supply chain (training data, fine-tuning, and RAG sources).
plain.AC.2.3: Each tool passes adversarial robustness testing (deliberate attacks) before onboarding and after any material model or system-prompt change, including prompt-injection probes, jailbreak suites, and indirect injection via realistic PRs and issues.
plain.AC.2.4: Evaluations follow a recognized framework such as NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, or ISO/IEC 42001, and are repeated after a major version change, a vendor incident, or new threat intelligence relevant to the tool.
plain.AC.3.1: Written guidance forbids putting secrets, credentials, personal data (PII), or classified data in any prompt sent to an AI tool, and it is enforced in pre-commit hooks, editor (IDE) integrations, and CI (the automated build checks).
plain.AC.3.2: Technical controls automatically strip sensitive material from any context sent to an AI tool, such as redaction on the developer's machine, approved context filters, or secret scanners that run before each prompt.
plain.AC.3.3: Outside context fed to an AI tool is treated as untrusted and screened for prompt injection first: PR descriptions and comments, fork diffs, issue bodies, commit messages, third-party documentation, web search results, and MCP tool outputs.
plain.AC.3.4: The AI tool enforces an instruction hierarchy in which system and developer messages take precedence over untrusted repository content, and this holds across multi-turn conversations and workflows where the AI uses tools.
plain.AC.3.5: Input length controls stop untrusted PR or repository content from crowding system instructions or safety directives out of what the AI can see; oversized inputs are rejected outright, never silently cut short.
plain.AC.3.6: Prompts and AI responses are encrypted in transit and at rest and kept per the data-classification policy, and tenants and projects are cryptographically separated from each other.
plain.AC.4.1: AI-generated code is always reviewed by a qualified human engineer who is not the same person who asked for the AI generation (separation of duties), and the AI agent itself never counts as the human reviewer.
plain.AC.4.2: Automated security testing (SAST, IAST, DAST, secret scanning, IaC scanning, and SCA) runs on every pull request containing AI-generated code, with AI-attribution-aware rules turned on where the scanner supports them.
plain.AC.4.3: Pull requests containing AI-generated code are blocked from merging when an automated scan reports a critical security finding (CVSS 9.0 or higher, or the organization's equivalent), unless an authorized human approves a written exception.
plain.AC.4.4: Security-critical files AI generated or modified need stricter review, like two-person review or security-team sign-off: authentication, authorization, and crypto code, IAM policy, CI/CD workflows, deployment manifests, and sandbox or network rules.
plain.AC.4.5: Differential fuzz testing or property-based tests (automated tests that try many generated inputs) cover the security-critical behaviors of AI-generated code: input validation, authorization logic, and deserialization safety.
plain.AC.5.1: Prompt-and-response pairs are logged with stable correlation identifiers, so an investigator can later replay the whole chain from prompt to response, commit, build, and deployment.
plain.AC.5.2: Developers can pull up the citations that support a suggestion (training snippets, retrieved documents, and MCP tool outputs), and the citation chain travels with the artifact.
plain.AC.5.3: Explainability reports, AI-event logs, and citation records are kept in tamper-evident storage (append-only, write-once, or an immutable log store) and are referred to during security reviews.
plain.AC.6.1: Developers and reviewers can flag insecure or non-compliant suggestions, and each flag is tracked to closure, linked back to the originating prompt and response and forward to any downstream artifacts.
plain.AC.6.2: Aggregated feedback feeds periodic system-prompt updates or retrieval from vetted secure-coding sources (OWASP Cheat Sheets, internal coding standards), plus fine-tuning on that feedback where the organization controls model training.
plain.AC.6.3: Scheduled red-team exercises attack the AI tooling itself with direct and indirect prompt injection via realistic PRs, issues, and comments, jailbreak corpora, and supply-chain payload generation; findings are fixed under tracked severity deadlines.
plain.AC.6.4: A closed-loop evaluation harness runs regression tests after every fine-tune, system-prompt change, or model upgrade, and security metrics must meet or exceed the prior baseline before deployment.
plain.AC.7.1: AI-generated or AI-modified artifacts are clearly labeled and tracked as such, including infrastructure-as-code, CI/CD workflow files, container and orchestration manifests, and security policy artifacts.
plain.AC.7.2: AI-generated infrastructure and pipeline configurations need human review and approval before they run in any environment beyond a hermetic (fully sealed-off) sandbox.
plain.AC.7.3: AI-generated infrastructure and workflow changes pass policy-as-code enforcement (automated rule checks such as OPA, Checkov, or tfsec) at least as strict as for human-authored changes, and policy violations block promotion.
plain.AC.7.4: Changes to high-impact pipeline triggers (pull_request_target, workflow_run, self-hosted runner labels, workflow permissions, OIDC trust policies, and secret-environment mappings) need dual control and security-team review, whoever made them.
plain.AC.7.5: Drift detection compares deployed infrastructure and live workflow configurations against signed, AI-attributed baselines and alerts on any unauthorized modification.
plain.AC.8.1: Autonomous agents cannot approve, merge, sign, or deploy artifacts they generated themselves, and this is enforced by the source-control system, the CI system, and the artifact registry, not by policy alone.
plain.AC.8.2: AI systems run under scoped, non-human identities (such as service accounts or short-lived tokens), and those identities cannot promote their own generated artifacts across environments.
plain.AC.8.3: Autonomous agents cannot bypass branch protection, required reviews, required status checks, signed-commit requirements, or merge queues, and any agent attempt to change these settings raises a security alert.
plain.AC.8.4: Separation of duties holds across the stages of an AI-generated change: generation, review, approval, and deployment are each performed by a distinct principal, human or system.
plain.AC.9.1: AI-generated artifacts carry signed origin and generation metadata (such as SLSA provenance or AI BOM entries) naming the AI system that produced them, the generation context, the humans involved, and the associated audit records.
plain.AC.9.2: Deployment pipelines check that origin and generation metadata on AI-generated artifacts is present, signed, and intact before promotion, using a trusted verifier such as Sigstore/cosign or in-toto verification.
plain.AC.9.3: Artifacts are rejected at deployment and quarantined for review when required origin and generation information is missing, they are signed by untrusted keys, or they come from an unapproved AI system or environment.
plain.AC.10.1: AI-generated artifacts carry the required origin and generation fields: model identity and version, tool or agent identity, generation context, prompt hash, human involvement, session identifiers, and correlation IDs.
plain.AC.10.2: Origin and generation metadata is checked for completeness and consistency: no missing or ambiguous fields, values normalized to a single form, and a signature chain that validates back to a trusted root.
plain.AC.10.3: The verifier rejects artifacts with incomplete, inconsistent, or unverifiable origin and generation metadata before merge or deployment, per SLSA and ISO/IEC 42001, and logs each rejection so trends can be tracked.
plain.AC.11.1: AI review and assistant bots treat all PR-supplied content (diff, title, description, comments, files, commit messages, linked URLs) as untrusted and apply the AISVS C2.1 prompt-injection defenses: instruction hierarchy, sanitization, and indirect-injection detection.
plain.AC.11.2: AI review and assistant bot system prompts and policy configurations are integrity-checked at load time (signed or hash-pinned), and nothing in the repository, branches, PR-sourced environment variables, or other user input can modify them.
plain.AC.11.3: AI review and assistant bots emit only structured, schema-validated output (JSON with allowed fields and actions), and free-form output is treated as untrusted and never run as a command, query, shell snippet, or workflow step.
plain.AC.11.4: AI review and assistant bots run in network-isolated, least-privilege sandboxes: a dedicated namespace, outbound traffic denied except to approved APIs, no mounted repository secrets, and only short-lived credentials.
plain.AC.11.5: Every privileged action a bot can take (approving, merging, labeling, dismissing reviews, commenting outside its sandbox, or invoking external tools) goes through a separate, audited authorization path decided by a policy engine, not the LLM.
plain.AC.11.6: AI review and assistant bots log all prompts (including outside context), tool calls, and outputs to tamper-evident storage, and outbound traffic (URLs, IPs, DNS, payload sizes) is watched for data theft, with alerts tuned for webhook, paste-site, and bin-service destinations.
plain.AC.11.7: For untrusted fork PRs, AI review bots run in a zero-privilege, read-only shadow mode, with restricted code-generation comments and no privileged workflow actions, until a maintainer clears a first-time-contributor verification gate.
plain.AC.11.8: AI review and assistant bots get continuous adversarial testing that replays indirect-prompt-injection corpora through simulated PRs, issues, and comments; detection is tracked over time, and a regression blocks the update that caused it.
plain.AC.12.1: Workflows triggered by untrusted contributions (such as pull_request_target or workflow_run) never check out, build, test, or run untrusted code with write permissions or any secrets; a privileged follow-up gets only validated passive artifacts from an unprivileged pull_request workflow.
plain.AC.12.2: Secrets, credentials, and pipeline job tokens are not persisted into workspaces that process AI-touched or fork-originated untrusted code, for example by setting persist-credentials: false and scrubbing cached credentials from CI runners.
plain.AC.12.3: Secrets are not exposed to workflows running code from forks or first-time contributors: platform environment-protection rules require manual approval before any secret-bearing job runs, and bot-level controls (AC.11.7) do not substitute.
plain.AC.12.4: Self-hosted or persistent runners used by AI tooling are ephemeral (destroyed after each job), network-segmented, and isolated from production credentials, and long-lived runners never process fork PRs or AI-generated untrusted artifacts.
plain.AC.12.5: Changes to workflow definition files (such as .github/workflows) are detected on every PR and go through elevated review that includes a security reviewer, whoever the contributor and whether or not AI was involved; AI agents cannot bypass it.
plain.AC.12.6: Pipeline audit logs stream in real time to central security monitoring, with rules tuned for AI-augmented threats: bulk PRs from new accounts, workflow-file changes in fork PRs, unexpected secret access from AI runners, and unusual outbound traffic from AI workloads.
plain.AC.12.7: A privileged follow-up workflow treats artifacts from untrusted PR workflows as untrusted passive data and never executes binaries, scripts, packages, caches, or generated workflow fragments that came from an untrusted contribution.
plain.AC.12.8: Remediation of a vulnerable workflow includes invalidating or re-validating every PR opened before the fix landed, so a later commit to such a PR cannot pick up the stale workflow definition and route around the fix.
plain.AC.13.1: Contribution-velocity and contributor-reputation analytics flag anomalies: bulk PRs from new accounts, coordinated fork waves just before PRs, PR volumes inconsistent with human authorship, and payload patterns reused across unrelated repositories.
plain.AC.13.2: PRs from first-time or low-reputation contributors need maintainer approval before any privileged workflow processes them, including AI review bots, secret-bearing jobs, and external-integration calls.
plain.AC.13.3: Automated PR gates detect known signs of AI-assisted malicious payloads: typosquatted or look-alike dependency names, package references with no published version, and dependencies whose creation, publication, or maintainer-change dates look anomalous for the PR.
plain.AC.13.4: Detection rules are tagged to MITRE ATT&CK (T1195 Supply Chain Compromise and CI/CD-relevant sub-techniques) and MITRE ATLAS techniques, maintained for inbound contribution analysis, and reviewed against current threat intelligence.
