plain.AC.13.5: Confirmed or high-confidence adversarial contributions trigger automated containment (block the PR, quarantine the fork, suspend the contributor, notify maintainers, freeze affected workflow files), and triage decisions feed back into detection.
plain.AC.13.6: PR analytics include code-structure (AST) profiling and style or entropy heuristics tuned to spot LLM-generated code; since this is still maturing, human review of flagged PRs, sandboxed runs of suspect payloads, and deferred merge are accepted in place of precise automated detection.
plain.AC.14.1: An incident-response playbook for AI-in-pipeline compromise covers revoking AI-agent credentials, rotating exposed secrets, quarantining compromised artifacts, notifying downstream consumers and any regulators, and keeping prompts, responses, and audit logs for forensics.
plain.AC.14.2: Any secret that touched a workflow run tied to a suspicious PR, a prompt-injection event, or an AI-agent anomaly is automatically rotated, and downstream issuers (cloud IAM, package registries, signing-key custodians) are notified.
plain.AC.14.3: AI agent identities (keys, tokens, OIDC trust grants) can be rapidly revoked and quarantined, with a written target time-to-revoke that is tested at least once a year.
plain.AC.14.4: During incident response, build provenance and AI BOM records are used to identify every downstream artifact produced under the suspect AI agent or compromised pipeline run, so recall, rebuild, or quarantine can be targeted.
plain.AC.14.5: Automated remediation is tested in tabletop or live-fire exercises at least once a year, with scenarios including a prompt-injected reviewer bot, fork-PR secret exfiltration, and an AI-generated malicious workflow file.
plain.SBD-AS-01: The system is split into trust zones (separate network areas, called Spaces) that are enforced, and traffic between zones flows only through a governed integration layer, such as a gateway or message bus.
plain.SBD-AS-02: Services are addressed and discovered in one unified, consistent way across environments, and shortcuts that work only inside a zone are not used from outside it.
plain.SBD-AS-03: Each service has clear boundaries, is right-sized for its job, and owns its own data, and no services depend on each other in a circle (circular dependencies).
plain.SBD-AS-04: The architecture avoids long synchronous chains of services each waiting on the next, and uses event-driven or queued handoffs instead where appropriate.
plain.SBD-AS-05: The contracts for APIs and events (the agreed formats services exchange) are defined and versioned, and consumers are notified before breaking changes take effect.
plain.SBD-AS-06: Messaging is durable (messages are persisted, replicated, and retained), with a defined strategy for the dead-letter queue (DLQ, where undeliverable messages go) and for triage of what lands there.
plain.SBD-AS-07: Services start up safely when a dependency is missing, and autoscaling (adding or removing copies as load changes) is defined with a minimum number of replicas.
plain.SBD-AS-08: Legacy integrations are isolated behind an anti-corruption layer (a translator that keeps an old system's quirks out of new code), and a migration path is defined.
plain.SBD-DM-01: Data are classified, each class has named owners, and the controls protecting data are proportional to its classification.
plain.SBD-DM-02: Encryption is designed in, both in transit (TLS or mutual TLS) and at rest, with managed keys and key rotation.
plain.SBD-DM-03: Handlers and workflows are idempotent (handling the same request twice has the same effect as once), and duplicate detection or suppression is in place where needed.
plain.SBD-DM-04: Transactions across services use Sagas (steps that each have a compensating step to undo them), two-phase commit (2PC) is avoided, and ordinary ACID transactions within one service are preferred first.
plain.SBD-DM-05: Each class of data has retention and deletion policies, and minimization is applied, so only the data needed is collected and stored.
plain.SBD-DM-06: The consistency model (how up to date each copy of the data is) is documented, the user experience handles stale data and conflicts, and event sourcing is considered where appropriate.
plain.SBD-RR-01: Retries wait longer after each failure (exponential backoff) plus a small random delay (jitter), and default exception handling and safe error models exist.
plain.SBD-RR-02: Circuit breakers and bulkheads (which stop calls to a failing dependency and keep failures contained) protect dependencies, and non-critical features have fallback or degraded modes.
plain.SBD-RR-03: Asynchronous messaging semantics are defined, including ordering, delivery guarantees, and acknowledgment and visibility timeouts, and dead-letter queues (DLQs) are monitored.
plain.SBD-RR-04: Shared integration layers, such as a gateway or message bus, are highly available and contain errors, so a failure does not spread from one zone to another.
plain.SBD-RR-05: Every endpoint that changes data enforces an Idempotency-Key (so a repeated request is not applied twice), and concurrency controls, such as locks or optimistic concurrency, are in place.
plain.SBD-RR-06: All calls have timeouts, services have health probes, and critical paths have explicit failover strategies, such as running across multiple availability zones (multi-AZ).
plain.SBD-RR-07: Quotas and autoscaling are defined, rate limits are enforced at the edges where traffic comes in, and the minimum capacity is documented.
plain.SBD-RR-08: Caching, a CDN (content delivery network), and back-pressure (slowing senders when the system is overloaded) are applied where appropriate, and performance guardrails are defined.
plain.SBD-AC-01: All communications use TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS), and each service's identity is verified, for example with certificates issued by a service mesh.
plain.SBD-AC-02: A central identity provider (IdP, using OIDC or OAuth2) is used, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced on privileged and admin paths, and tokens are short-lived.
plain.SBD-AC-03: Role- or attribute-based access control (RBAC or ABAC) governs the APIs and who may publish or consume messages, and least privilege (only the access needed) is applied.
plain.SBD-AC-04: Authorization is centralized at the gateway or service mesh using policy-as-code (access rules written as code), and shared integration services are governed.
plain.SBD-AC-05: Secrets are stored in a secret manager, keys and certificates rotate automatically, and no secrets appear in code or logs.
plain.SBD-AC-06: The regulatory controls that apply, such as privacy or financial rules, are identified, with evidence that the design aligns with them.
plain.SBD-AC-07: Least privilege (only the access needed) extends to CI/CD build pipelines, version-control (VCS) apps, chat-ops, and third-party tooling, and periodic reviews are scheduled.
plain.SBD-MT-01: Logs are structured and centralized, carry correlation or trace IDs that link related entries, and administrative access is logged.
plain.SBD-MT-02: Metrics, service level objectives (SLOs), and dashboards cover service health and anomalies in event flow, and alerts are actionable.
plain.SBD-MT-03: The test strategy plans security tests aligned with ASVS, and negative tests (checking that what should fail does fail) drawn from threat modeling.
plain.SBD-MT-04: Secure by Design (SbD) controls are verifiable in tests, including isolation, mTLS, authorization denials, and rate-limit behavior.
plain.SBD-MT-05: API descriptions (OpenAPI and AsyncAPI) and event catalogs are published, and decision records (ADRs) and runbooks are kept current.
plain.SBD-MT-06: A documented Incident Response plan, covering roles, communications, and evidence handling, exists and is rehearsed.
plain.SBD-MT-07: Audit log retention of at least 12 months is defined, with tamper-evidence (changes can be detected) and a searchable hot window of recent logs.
